As such, the expiries today are likely to reinforce those levels unless there are any major headline surprises to shift broader market sentiment and the dollar.

item.title: Major central banks take centre stage this week but will there be any surprises?
item.description:
The central bank bonanza is back in town this week, with five big names lining up to announce their latest monetary policy decisions. After all the recent drama involving oil prices, bond yields, and the stock market, perhaps it is time for central bankers to have their say again.

Of note, we will have the RBNZ, BOC, Fed, ECB, and BOJ all on the agenda this week. And looking to market pricing, traders seem to have a pretty good idea of what to expect already from the decisions to come. So, the only question is will there be any surprises? Let's see.

The RBNZ will kick things off on Wednesday with traders fully pricing in a 25 bps rate hike. That leaves little suspense surrounding the decision itself, although traders will be watching for clues on whether policymakers are prepared to tighten further in December.

Then, the BOC will follow later in the day with markets pricing in roughly 83% odds of a 25 bps rate hike. The pricing reflects relatively strong conviction with just a bit of room for a potential surprise. But all else being equal, the central bank should deliver as expected this week. Perhaps the bigger question is whether another rate hike will be needed as policymakers continue to wrestle with inflation risks. So, that will be the key risk trigger for the loonie reaction in the aftermath.

After that, we will have the Fed to finish off the day with traders assigning around 91% odds of no change in interest rates. As such, the decision itself won't be the main talking point here. Instead, it will all rest on Fed chair Warsh's pess conference. His remarks will be closely scrutinised, especially with rising oil prices complicating the inflation outlook while recent weakness in the stock market raises fresh concerns about growth.

And on Thursday, it is then on the ECB to take the wheel with markets pricing in roughly 90% odds of a hold. But with energy-driven inflation pressures building and European growth showing signs of weakness, ECB president Lagarde will have a lot to address with her press conference. In particular, traders will be looking for clues on December, where expectations for another rate hike have been building.

Finally, the BOJ will round things off on Friday with traders seeing roughly 98% odds of no change in interest rates. But with the yen still struggling and underlying inflation holding near 2%, the focus will be on whether policymakers offer any stronger signals about a potential move in December. BOJ governor Ueda's press conference is likely to steer clear of any pre-commitment though, so there might not be much to the key risk event here; all else being equal.

All things considered, I wouldn't expect the interest rate decisions alone to deliver much drama this week. As we've seen time and again, it is often what central bankers say about their next move that ends up stirring markets the most. So, that is what I'll be watching more closely with the meeting decisions and press conferences this week.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

Oil

Oil prices opened with a gap lower on Monday after a weekend in which the US did not escalate the war with Iran, easing back from the near six-month highs reached late last week. Losses were limited, however, as ongoing attacks on Saudi Arabia kept supply concerns in focus.

Fresh news flow was thin during the session. Later, two sources told Reuters that senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan were expected to meet Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday to discuss regional coordination.

Separately, Saudi Arabia and Singapore said Saudi crude will be stored in underground caverns on Singapore’s Jurong Island from the second half of 2027, aimed at strengthening Asian supply security while Strait of Hormuz flows remain disrupted. Saudi Aramco is due to sign a memorandum of understanding with Singapore’s Energy Market Authority and Jurong Group, with talks targeted to conclude within months.

Gold

Gold hovered near a three-month low as investors awaited this week’s Federal Reserve meeting for signals on the US rate outlook. Elevated energy prices have reinforced expectations that the Fed will keep rates higher for longer, raising the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding bullion. Gold fell about 4% last week and briefly dipped below $4,000. On the structural side, Goldman Sachs estimates central banks bought 79 tonnes in August, more than four times the pre-2022 monthly average, with some reserves shifting from New York to London.

FX

Currency markets were largely subdued, although USD/JPY showed some volatility within a modest range, moving from above 157.10 to below 156.75. China’s onshore yuan strengthened in early trade to its firmest level since June 9, 2022.

Equities

Regional stock markets were mostly lower, with South Korea leading the declines:

  • South Korea’s Kospi: down 1.6%
  • South Korea’s Kosdaq: down 2.8%
  • China’s Shanghai Composite: down 0.3%
  • Hong Kong’s Hang Seng: up 0.2%

In Tokyo, chip and electronics shares led the declines. Earlier, Goldman Sachs cut its 12-month Kospi target to 9,000 from 12,000, though it said the index still has more than 60% upside after a slide of over 35% from its June peak.

Brazil

President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won Brazil’s presidential runoff on Sunday, defeating right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro to secure a fourth non-consecutive term after trailing in the first round. A Tokyo-listed exchange-traded fund tracking the Bovespa fell nearly 15% in Asian trade on the result. Goldman Sachs said an extreme scenario on Monday could see USD/BRL rise 10%, long-term government bond yields climb about 200 basis points, credit spreads widen 30 to 40 basis points and Brazilian equities fall around 15%.

Other news

In Serbia, Aleksandar Vučić, who has served as both prime minister and president over nearly 12 years, conceded defeat to the student-led protest movement following Sunday’s snap parliamentary election.

In crypto, Strategy chairman Michael Saylor did not post his usual Sunday bitcoin chart, which has typically preceded the company’s purchase announcements. Some market watchers took this as a possible sign that Strategy, the largest corporate holder of bitcoin, paused its buying last week, though the absence of a chart is not confirmation. Saylor was active on X, describing bitcoin as “the moat” in a reply to Jack Dorsey. The company’s Monday filing should clarify its activity, and its third-quarter results are due on Thursday.

Elsewhere, Elon Musk said SpaceX has closed $40 billion in debt financing for GPUs, and warned that tightening credit could force failures and consolidation among AI-focused neocloud providers. China’s commerce ministry said it reserves the right to take countermeasures against a proposed US Treasury rule widening curbs on American investment in Chinese technology.

Week ahead

It is a heavy week for central banks. The Reserve Bank of New Zealand and the Bank of Canada are both expected to hike on Wednesday, while the Fed, also deciding on Wednesday, is expected to hold. The European Central Bank on Thursday and the Bank of Japan, which meets on Thursday and Friday, are both expected to keep rates unchanged. In Australia, RBA Assistant Governor Sarah Hunter said on Sunday the bank has not yet done enough to tame inflation, ahead of Wednesday’s CPI data and the November 3 policy meeting.

item.title: Brazil ETF tumbles nearly 15% in Tokyo after Lula’s comeback runoff win
item.description:
The Tokyo ETF move is an early and thin-volume signal, so the real test comes when Brazilian markets open, with the real, the local rates curve and the Bovespa likely to bear the brunt of any repricing. Goldman Sachs’ figures describe an extreme scenario rather than a base case, but they frame the scale of the potential move, with the long end of the curve and the currency most exposed. Positioning matters: markets rallied after the first round on expectations of a different outcome, so some of the selling may reflect that trade being unwound rather than a fresh view on policy. Spillover to other Latin American currencies and EM risk sentiment is possible if the selloff is disorderly, while a contained reaction could see dip-buyers emerge quickly.

---

Lula pulled off a rare second-round comeback, and the first verdict from markets, a near 15% drop in a Tokyo-listed Brazil ETF, suggests investors had been positioned for the other result.

Summary:

  • Lula won Brazil’s presidential runoff on Sunday against Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, securing a fourth non-consecutive term with about 52% to 48% and a margin of more than 4 million votes, with nearly all ballots counted
  • He trailed in the October 4 first round, making him the first candidate since 1989 to lose round one and win the presidency
  • A Tokyo-listed ETF tracking the Bovespa fell nearly 15% in Asian trade on the result
  • Goldman Sachs said an extreme scenario could see USD/BRL rise 10%, long-term government bond yields climb about 200bp, credit spreads widen 30 to 40bp and equities fall about 15%

Brazilian assets face a sharp repricing after President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won Sunday’s runoff election, with an early read from Asian trading pointing to heavy selling when local markets open.

Lula defeated right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro by about 52% to 48%, a margin of more than 4 million votes with nearly all ballots counted, securing a fourth non-consecutive term. The result marked a comeback: Lula trailed in the first round on October 4, making him the first candidate since 1989 to lose the opening round and go on to win the presidency.

The initial market response was stark. A Tokyo-listed exchange-traded fund tracking Brazil’s Bovespa index fell nearly 15% in Asian trade on news of the victory, according to Reuters. While trading in such offshore vehicles can be thin, the move offers an early indication of how investors may react across Brazilian assets.

Goldman Sachs set out what an extreme scenario could look like on Monday. The bank said the dollar could rise as much as 10% against the real, long-term government bond yields could climb by about 200 basis points, credit spreads could widen by 30 to 40 basis points and Brazilian equities could fall around 15%. Goldman framed these as an extreme case rather than its central expectation, but the figures underline the scale of the repricing risk.

Part of the pressure reflects positioning. Brazilian markets rallied after the first round, when Bolsonaro finished ahead, as investors priced in a higher chance of his victory. Sunday’s result reverses that assumption, leaving those trades exposed.

Attention now turns to the opening of Brazilian markets, where the real, local interest rate futures and the Bovespa will show whether the selling matches the scale signalled in Tokyo or proves more contained. Investors will also watch for early signals from Lula’s camp on economic and fiscal policy for the new term, which could help determine whether the initial reaction extends or stabilises. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Saudi Arabia to store crude in Singapore caverns from 2027 as Hormuz disruption bites
item.description:
The arrangement will not add barrels before the second half of 2027, so the near-term price impact is limited, but it signals that producers and consumers expect Strait of Hormuz risk to persist well beyond the current war. Storage closer to Asian refiners would give Saudi Arabia a buffer to keep supplying key customers during future disruptions, helping defend its market share in the region against rival suppliers. Over time, a strategic stockpile in Singapore could reduce the risk premium Asian buyers pay during supply scares and strengthen the city-state’s role as a regional pricing and trading hub. For now, oil markets remain driven by the immediate disruption to Hormuz flows, which this deal does not address.

---

With the Strait of Hormuz no longer a safe bet, Saudi Arabia is planning to park its crude on Asia’s doorstep.

Summary:

  • Saudi Arabia plans to store crude in underground caverns on Singapore’s Jurong Island from the second half of 2027, the two countries’ energy ministers said on Monday
  • The announcement at Singapore International Energy Week aims to strengthen regional supply security as the US-Israeli war with Iran severely disrupts Strait of Hormuz flows
  • Before the conflict, about two-thirds of Asia’s crude came from the Middle East
  • Saudi Aramco is due to sign an MoU on Monday with Singapore’s Energy Market Authority and Jurong Group, with negotiations targeted to conclude within months
  • Singapore says the arrangement will boost the resilience of Saudi supply chains in Southeast Asia and its own energy security during disruptions

Saudi Arabia plans to store crude oil in underground caverns on Singapore’s Jurong Island from the second half of 2027, in a move aimed at strengthening energy supply security across Asia as the war with Iran continues to disrupt shipments through the Strait of Hormuz.

The plan was announced on Monday by the energy ministers of Saudi Arabia and Singapore at Singapore International Energy Week. Singapore’s minister responsible for energy said the two countries had agreed in principle to set up the arrangement, which would make Saudi supply chains in Southeast Asia more resilient while also supporting Singapore’s own energy security in the event of supply disruptions.

Saudi Aramco is due to sign a memorandum of understanding on Monday with Singapore’s Energy Market Authority and Jurong Group, the state-linked developer of the island’s industrial estate. The parties aim to conclude negotiations within a few months.

The announcement reflects the strain the conflict has placed on Asia’s energy supplies. The US-Israeli war with Iran has severely disrupted flows through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway that carries much of the Gulf’s crude exports. Before the war, about two-thirds of Asia’s crude oil came from the Middle East, leaving the region’s refiners and governments heavily exposed to any interruption.

Holding Saudi crude in Singapore would place supplies within reach of major Asian buyers, giving the kingdom a way to keep serving customers if Gulf export routes are blocked or delayed. For Singapore, already a major refining and oil trading centre, the caverns would add a strategic buffer to its energy system.

The storage will not begin operating until the second half of 2027, so it offers no relief from the current disruption. But the deal suggests that both producers and consumers are preparing for a longer period in which Gulf supply routes can no longer be taken for granted, and further arrangements of this kind may follow as Asian importers look to diversify their exposure.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman’s 79-tonne central bank gold estimate goes mainstream as reserves shift to London
item.description:
Heavy official-sector buying offers a structural cushion beneath gold just as speculative liquidation has dragged prices below $4,000, and it supports the argument that dips are being absorbed by long-term buyers. It does not guarantee a floor, however: near-term direction still depends on oil, yields and Fed expectations, and central bank demand did not prevent last week’s slide. The gap between Goldman’s flow-based estimate and officially reported purchases suggests accumulation may be larger than disclosed, which matters for the longer-run supply-demand balance. The shift of holdings from New York to London is a reserve-management story rather than an immediate price driver, but it adds to debate over the dollar’s role in official portfolios.

---

Earlier:

  • Gold dips below $4,000 as long liquidation swamps ETF buying, Saxo Bank says
  • Gold dips below $4,000 in worst week in four months as oil fuels Fed hike fears

---

While speculators dump gold, central banks are quietly buying it at a multiple of their old pace, and some are deciding they would rather keep it in London than New York.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs estimates central banks bought 79 tonnes of gold in August, more than four times the pre-2022 average of 17 tonnes a month, and up from its 44-tonne estimate for July
  • On a three-month seasonally adjusted basis, purchases are running at about 85 tonnes a month; China was the largest identifiable buyer at an estimated 25 tonnes, above the roughly 20 tonnes it reported
  • The estimate, first reported by investingLive on October 19, gained wider attention after Fortune highlighted it last week
  • Holdings at the New York Fed fell by 40 tonnes while those at the Bank of England rose 46; the Dutch central bank moved 86 tonnes out of New York and Ottawa to London
  • Goldman views central bank demand as a structural support for gold, even as prices have fallen below $4,000

Central banks are buying gold at more than four times their historical pace and shifting some of their holdings out of the United States, a trend first flagged by Goldman Sachs research that is now attracting wider attention.

As investingLive reported on October 19, Goldman Sachs estimates that central banks bought 79 tonnes of gold in August, well above the pre-2022 average of 17 tonnes a month and a sharp step up from the bank’s 44-tonne estimate for July. On a three-month seasonally adjusted basis, purchases are running at around 85 tonnes a month. China was the largest identifiable buyer, with an estimated 25 tonnes, above the roughly 20 tonnes officially reported by the People’s Bank of China. The findings were picked up last week by Fortune, which framed them as central banks quietly stockpiling gold at four times the usual rate.

Goldman builds its estimate from trade and flow data rather than relying solely on official disclosures. That helps explain why it runs well above the World Gold Council’s count of reported net central bank purchases for August, and it is consistent with the bank’s view that some buying, particularly by China, is running ahead of official figures.

The second part of the story is where the gold is held. Holdings at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York fell by 40 tonnes over the period, while those at the Bank of England rose by 46 tonnes, pointing to a shift in storage from New York to London. The Dutch central bank separately confirmed it spent six months moving 86 tonnes of gold out of New York and Ottawa to London. Those transfers relocate existing reserves rather than adding new demand.

Goldman continues to see central bank buying as a structural support for the gold market rather than a passing phase. That backdrop is notable given recent price action, with gold falling below $4,000 last week as speculative selling, higher oil prices and rate concerns weighed. The official-sector data suggest long-term buyers have kept accumulating even as short-term positioning has been unwound. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BOJ to hold at 1.25%, but Ueda signals further hikes toward neutral
item.description:
With a hold widely expected, yen and JGB moves are likely to hinge on the vote and Ueda’s guidance. Hawkish dissent from Takata or Tamura, or language pointing to the next meeting, would probably bring December pricing forward and offer the yen some support. A unanimous hold paired with cautious messaging could see hike expectations drift toward January, keeping the yen soft. Front-end JGB yields remain the most sensitive gauge of shifts in timing, and Friday’s Tokyo CPI print lands on the same day as the decision, adding to the potential for volatility.

---

Earlier:

  • ING sees BOJ holding at 1.25%, two hikes in 2027
  • BOJ preview: Daiwa sees hold, but 2% inflation call could open door to December hike

---

Ueda is in no rush to hike again this week, but he has made clear the BOJ is not done, with the debate now about whether the next move comes in December or January.

Summary:

  • The BOJ is expected to keep its policy rate at 1.25% at its October 29-30 meeting, after hiking from 1% in a 7-2 vote in September
  • Ueda has signalled that back-to-back hikes are not needed, but said that with underlying inflation close to 2%, the bank can no longer tolerate further increases and must stabilise it around target
  • The likely path is a hike to 1.50% in December or January, then 1.75% in March or April
  • Hawks Takata and Tamura may begin pushing for the next hike on Friday, setting up a possible move on December 17-18; dovish members Asada and Sato have dissented against recent hikes
  • Tokyo October CPI is forecast at 2.7% to 2.8% across the key measures, with September jobs, industrial output and retail sales also due

The Bank of Japan is expected to leave its policy rate unchanged at 1.25% at its October 29-30 meeting, with Governor Kazuo Ueda signalling there is no need for back-to-back increases but that rates will have to rise further toward a neutral level, according to Mace News.

The board raised the rate from 1% in a 7-2 vote in September. Since then, Ueda has said that oversized or consecutive hikes are typically reserved for situations where inflation is rising rapidly beyond target, and that the bank is making pre-emptive adjustments to avoid being forced into abrupt tightening later. Speaking in Bangkok on October 16, he said that with underlying inflation now close to 2%, the bank can no longer tolerate further increases and its main goal is to stabilise inflation around that level. Board member Junko Koeda also argued last week that the bank should not become overly cautious about raising rates.

Mace News sees the most likely path as a hike to 1.50% in December or January, followed by a rise to 1.75% in March or April. That would continue a faster pattern of tightening every three to four months.

The board is broadly divided into four camps. Hawks Hajime Takata and Naoki Tamura may start pushing for the next increase on Friday, setting the stage for possible action at the December 17-18 meeting. At the dovish end, Toichiro Asada and Ayano Sato have dissented against recent hikes.

On the data front, Tokyo’s October CPI is forecast to show inflation at 2.7% to 2.8% across all three key measures, partly reflecting the fading impact of local fiscal support. September jobs, industrial production and retail sales figures are also due.

item.title: Gold dips below $4,000 as long liquidation swamps ETF buying, Saxo Bank says
item.description:
The split between fast-money selling and steady ETF accumulation leaves gold finely balanced: if long liquidation is close to exhausted, structural buyers could provide a base, but a decisive break of trendline support would likely trigger another round of technical selling. This week’s Fed decision and oil prices are the near-term catalysts, since any renewed jump in energy costs that lifts rate expectations would add pressure. A gold-silver ratio above 74 signals that markets are pricing industrial demand risk and broader de-risking, leaving silver more exposed if equities wobble. Speculative positioning has already been pared, which reduces some of the forced-selling risk from here.

---

Earlier:

  • Gold dips below $4,000 in worst week in four months as oil fuels Fed hike fears

---

Gold’s slide below $4,000 is a positioning story more than a fundamentals one, with speculators heading for the exits while long-term ETF investors keep buying.

Summary:

  • Saxo Bank said gold’s drop is notable because it came alongside a strong rally in US Treasuries, with momentum selling and long liquidation overwhelming the usual support from lower yields
  • Spot gold briefly fell below $4,000 after Thursday’s break of support around $4,060 accelerated technical selling, putting it on course for its steepest weekly drop in months
  • Silver fell toward an 11-month low near $54, pushing the gold-silver ratio above 74, also an 11-month high
  • ETF investors have kept accumulating gold almost uninterrupted since July, and Saxo Bank says the correction does not necessarily invalidate the longer-term case
  • Support sits at an ascending trendline near $3,985, with resistance around $4,060 and then $4,230

Gold’s slide below $4,000 an ounce is being driven by speculative selling rather than a breakdown in long-term demand, according to Saxo Bank, which said momentum-driven selling and long liquidation have outweighed influences that would normally support the metal.

The decline has been particularly striking because it has coincided with a powerful rally in US Treasuries, Saxo Bank said in a note. Falling bond yields would usually help gold, but this week the selling pressure has proved stronger. Spot gold briefly slipped below $4,000 during Friday’s Asian session after a break of support around $4,060 on Thursday accelerated technical selling. The metal was heading for its steepest weekly fall in several months and potentially its weakest weekly close since November, despite persistent geopolitical uncertainty and growing concern over the durability of the equity market rally.

Silver has fared worse, falling toward an 11-month low near $54. That has pushed the gold-silver ratio above 74, also an 11-month high, reflecting silver’s relative weakness amid broader risk reduction and worries about industrial demand.

Saxo Bank said the price action suggests short-term speculative selling is currently outweighing demand from longer-term investors, who have continued to build gold holdings through exchange-traded funds almost without pause since July, seeking protection against fiscal instability, currency debasement and geopolitical risk. A chart from the bank shows ETF holdings climbing back above roughly 100 million ounces, while speculative positions on COMEX have been pared back from recent highs.

The bank stressed that the correction does not necessarily undermine gold’s longer-term investment case, but said it shows that even assets with structural support can suffer sharp setbacks when speculative positions are unwound.

The focus now is on whether gold can stabilise. Saxo Bank highlighted an ascending trendline connecting the October 2025 and July 2026 lows, currently offering support near $3,985. The broken $4,060 level may act as initial resistance, ahead of a more significant barrier around $4,230. A lasting recovery is likely to require steadier energy prices, continued buying from central banks and ETF investors, and evidence that the recent wave of long liquidation has run its course.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Musk says SpaceX closed $40 billion GPU debt deal, predicts neocloud shakeout
item.description:
Musk’s warning lands on a sector already under pressure, and pure-play neocloud names such as CoreWeave and Nebius are likely to stay vulnerable as investors question their access to debt funding. The deal reinforces a widening split in AI financing, with diversified, investment-grade borrowers still able to raise capital while AI-dependent firms are squeezed. For Nvidia, the financing points to continued large-scale GPU demand into the first half of 2027. Credit markets will watch the final pricing and structure as a gauge of investor appetite for AI-linked debt.

---

Earlier:

  • Standard Chartered sees debt-funded share of AI capex rising to 40% in 2027 from 25%

--- SpaceX can still borrow $40 billion for AI chips on the strength of Starlink and launch revenue, and Musk says the AI-only neoclouds without that cushion are about to find out what that means.

Summary:

  • Musk said on Sunday that SpaceX has closed $40 billion in mostly callable debt financing for GPUs due to arrive in the first and second quarters of 2027, though it was unclear whether pricing had been agreed
  • He credited the company’s investment-grade status and Starlink and launch revenue; SpaceX expects fourth-quarter capex of $35 billion to $40 billion
  • Musk said debt markets have largely shut out companies without substantial revenue beyond AI data centres, predicting failures and consolidation among more than 200 neoclouds; he said SpaceX will not buy any
  • SpaceX’s AI unit is now its largest business, with third-quarter revenue up about ninefold to around $7.6 billion

Elon Musk said on Sunday that SpaceX has closed $40 billion in debt financing to buy graphics processing units, underscoring the scale of capital needed to build artificial intelligence computing capacity.

In posts on X, Musk said the financing was mainly callable debt for GPUs due to arrive in the first and second quarters of 2027, and would not be a major factor this quarter. He attributed the raise to SpaceX’s investment-grade status and its revenue from Starlink and rocket launches. It was not immediately clear whether investors had agreed on pricing. Bloomberg had reported that the deal could use a special purpose vehicle to keep the debt off SpaceX’s balance sheet, with Goldman Sachs leading talks with investors.

The financing follows rapid growth in SpaceX’s AI business, which is now its largest unit. item.title: ECB set to hold at 2.50% as Morgan Stanley sees December as natural moment for next hike
item.description:

The ECB looks set to take a breather this week, letting higher bond yields do some of its work, while December shapes up as the meeting where the next hike gets decided.

Summary:

  • The ECB announces its decision on Thursday and is widely expected to hold the deposit rate at 2.50% after hiking in September
  • Morgan Stanley says there is no evidence yet of significant indirect or second-round effects from the energy shock, and that higher long-term yields provide some extra tightening, removing the urgency to hike this week
  • The bank sees December, with new data and updated projections, as the more natural moment to change policy; a Reuters poll found 64 of 73 economists expect a December hike

The European Central Bank is widely expected to keep its deposit rate unchanged at 2.50% on Thursday, pausing after September’s rate increase as policymakers weigh an uncertain economic outlook against inflation that is still running well above target.

Morgan Stanley analysts said in a note that there is so far no sign of significant indirect or second-round effects from the latest energy shock on inflation, and that the recent rise in long-term bond yields is already providing a degree of additional tightening. Together, those factors remove any urgency to deliver another hike this week, the bank said, adding that December, when policymakers will have fresh data and updated staff projections, looks like the more natural moment to shift the policy stance.

That view is widely shared. In a Reuters poll conducted earlier this month, 70 of 73 economists expected the ECB to hold in October, while 64 of 73 saw a further 25 basis point increase in December, a sharp reversal from the previous survey, when most thought the tightening cycle was over.

The jump in sovereign bond yields, particularly in France amid concerns over its debt and budget, is likely to be on policymakers’ minds. ING economists argue that the French fiscal crisis and higher yields are already tightening financial conditions, making a hold very likely and pushing any further decision to December. Commerzbank expects the deposit rate to rise to 2.75% in December and then stay there throughout 2027, pointing to an anticipated decline in oil prices and the dampening effect of higher yields as reasons against further moves.

Investors will focus on President Christine Lagarde’s press conference for any signals on the prospect of further rate increases in the coming months. The decision is due at 13:15 GMT (09:15 ET), with the press conference following at 13:45 GMT (09:45 ET).

The data calendar is busy. Germany’s Ifo business survey for October is out on Monday, the GfK consumer confidence survey follows on Wednesday, and eurozone business and consumer surveys are due on Thursday. On Friday, provisional third-quarter eurozone GDP figures will be released alongside flash October inflation data from individual countries, including France and Germany, offering an early read on whether the case for a December hike is strengthening.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6691 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day’s closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point. A stronger-than-expected CNY midpoint is typically read as a sign the PBOC is leaning against depreciation pressure, while a weaker fixing for the CNY can indicate tolerance for a softer currency, often in response to dollar strength or domestic economic headwinds.In periods of heightened global volatility, such as shifts in US rate expectations, trade tensions or capital flow pressures, the fixing takes on added significance. For investors, it provides insight into Beijing’s currency priorities, balancing competitiveness, capital stability and financial market confidence.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

  • Oil above $100 a barrel on intensifying Middle East hostilities revived inflation fears and kept a December Fed hike in play

Gold heads into a pivotal week for US monetary policy on the back foot, after suffering its steepest weekly decline in more than four months and briefly slipping below $4,000 an ounce as surging oil prices revived inflation fears and reinforced expectations that the Federal Reserve will keep rates high.

The $4,000 level has become the market’s focal point. One analyst said speculators are defending it because a clean break would signal that markets have stopped pricing rate relief and started pricing sticky inflation, high yields and a stronger dollar. UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo struck a more constructive tone, saying that while gold could retest $4,000 in the near term, structural dip-buyers are expected to provide a firm floor around that level. Elsewhere in the complex, HSBC cut its average 2026 platinum and palladium price forecasts in a note last week, citing shifting market fundamentals and investor liquidation.

Attention now turns to the Fed, which announces its decision at 14:00 ET (18:00 GMT) on Wednesday after a two-day meeting. Markets heavily favour a hold at 3.75%-4.00% following September’s hike, leaving the statement and Chair’s press conference to set the tone on further tightening. item.title: Bitcoin ETF inflows fade as price pressure tests ETF buyers’ $81,300 cost basis
item.description:
Bitcoin ETF demand returned last week, then faded. Now price is testing the ETF buyers’ cost basis

Money came back into US spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds last week, but it didn’t stay. The funds took in about $1.07 billion over the first three sessions, then lost $773.5 million over the final two, according to preliminary Farside data. That left a provisional net inflow of $301.2 million for the week to October 23. Bitcoin, meanwhile, slipped back toward $80,000, close to the level where the average ETF buyer would start losing money.

---

Earlier:

  • Bitcoin buyers are fighting back, but sellers aren't finished. Here are the two prices swing traders should watch
  • Strategy bitcoin purchases shrink as buybacks take priority ahead of earnings

---

What happened

The week opened strongly. Spot bitcoin ETFs took in $526.7 million on Monday, $23.2 million on Tuesday and $524.8 million on Wednesday. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) led the way, drawing $665.2 million on Monday, its largest single-day inflow since October 2025.

The mood then reversed. Thursday brought $635.6 million in outflows, the largest daily withdrawal since June, followed by another $137.9 million on Friday. IBIT itself saw $254.1 million leave on Thursday and $110.3 million on Friday, though it still finished the week with net inflows of $565.7 million.

The week did end a run of two straight weeks of outflows. Even so, US spot bitcoin ETFs remain about $313.5 million in net outflows for October so far.

Why it matters

When investors buy shares in a spot bitcoin ETF, the fund buys bitcoin to back them. When they sell, the fund may sell bitcoin. That makes ETF flows a useful, if imperfect, gauge of demand through these products. They don’t show who is buying or why, and a strong day of inflows is not the same as a sustained trend.

The price response is the other half of the story. Bitcoin fell about 3.45% over the two days of outflows, and it briefly dipped below $80,000 over the weekend before recovering toward $80,600. Early-week inflows didn’t lift price meaningfully, and the late-week selling pushed it lower.

The level traders are watching

Coinbase Institutional has identified $80,000 to $82,000 as a key support zone. Its reasoning combines two reference points: an estimated average cost basis of $81,300 for ETF holders, and the 50-day moving average near $81,700.

The cost basis matters because it marks roughly where the typical ETF investor breaks even. While price holds above it, holders are sitting on modest gains. A sustained move below could leave many underwater, and some may choose to sell rather than wait. Coinbase warns that a lasting break below the zone could expose bitcoin to further losses toward $73,000 to $75,000.

A shift in who’s buying

There is a wider change in the background. Coinbase Institutional notes that corporate treasury companies bought about $14.5 billion of bitcoin in the first half of 2026, while US spot ETFs recorded nearly $5 billion in net selling. Since August, that has flipped: ETFs have attracted about $6.4 billion, against $1.5 billion for corporate treasuries.

That matters because the biggest corporate buyer, Strategy, has cut its weekly purchases to a few hundred coins in recent weeks. If ETFs are now the main source of steady demand, the swings in their flows carry more weight for price than they did earlier in the year.

The macro backdrop

Interest rates add another layer of risk. US producer prices rose 1.3% month on month in September, the largest increase since March 2022, and markets have raised the odds of a Federal Reserve rate hike in December. Higher rates tend to tighten financial conditions and make yield-paying assets more attractive than non-yielding ones such as bitcoin. That relationship is not fixed, but it is a headwind worth watching.

Ethereum went the other way

Ether ETFs had a weaker week, with $220.7 million in net outflows. BlackRock’s iShares Ethereum Trust (ETHA) accounted for $233.2 million of withdrawals, losing money on four straight days before a small inflow across the group on Friday.

What to watch next

The first thing to watch is whether bitcoin holds the $80,000 to $82,000 zone. A close back above the ETF cost basis, alongside renewed inflows, would suggest last week’s selling was a pause rather than a turn. Continued outflows while price trades below $81,300 would point to ETF holders cutting losses, and would put the $73,000 to $75,000 area in view.

The next week of Farside data will show which way it is breaking. Watch the flow trend and the price response together before treating any single day of inflows as a bullish signal. For traders, the practical point is that the ETF buyers’ cost basis has become a level with real behavioural weight: where many holders break even is often where their decisions change.

---

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

A week ago the Bank of Canada looked set to sit tight, but one hint from Governor Macklem about higher inflation forecasts has put a first hike in a year firmly on the table.

Summary:

  • The Bank of Canada announces its decision on Wednesday, with markets pricing an 81% chance of a 25bp hike to 2.50%, which would be its first move in a year
  • A Reuters poll found 19 of 34 economists expect a hike, and a majority see one more by March 2027; the previous poll had 80% expecting a hold through 2026
  • Governor Tiff Macklem said the bank’s inflation forecasts are likely to be revised higher, remarks markets read as a signal of tightening

  • TD does not share the market’s conviction, citing limited inflation breadth and near-term uncertainty

The Bank of Canada is expected to raise interest rates for the first time in a year on Wednesday, with markets pricing an 81% chance of a 25 basis point increase that would take its key policy rate to 2.50%, although some economists remain unconvinced the move is warranted.

Expectations have shifted rapidly. A Reuters poll conducted from October 21 to 23 found that 19 of 34 economists now forecast a hike this week, and a majority also expect one more increase by the end of March 2027, taking the rate to 2.75%. That marks a sharp reversal from the previous poll, when 80% of respondents expected the bank to hold at 2.25% through the end of 2026.

The catalyst was Governor Tiff Macklem, who told reporters that the bank’s quarterly inflation projections, to be published alongside Wednesday’s decision, are likely to be revised higher. Markets took the comments as a hint that tightening is coming, and futures pricing for an October hike jumped from around 30% before the remarks to roughly three in four, according to Reuters. Many economists switched their calls from a hold to a hike over the following week.

HSBC analysts said recent survey data suggest a hike is likely, pointing in particular to a rise in long-term consumer inflation expectations, even though other hard economic data have been on the soft side.

Not everyone agrees. TD analysts said they do not share the market’s conviction that rates will rise, citing limited breadth in inflation and uncertainty over the near-term outlook. Others have argued that energy-driven price increases are unlikely to feed through to underlying inflation on their own, while still expecting the bank to tighten if price pressures broaden. Weakness in the labour market earlier in the autumn had also led markets to push back expectations for a move toward December.

The decision and the accompanying Monetary Policy Report are due at 09:45 ET (13:45 GMT) on Wednesday. With a hike largely priced, the bank’s updated forecasts and guidance on further tightening are likely to drive the market reaction. August GDP data, due on Friday, will offer an early test of the outlook.

item.title: Standard Chartered sees debt-funded share of AI capex rising to 40% in 2027 from 25%
item.description:
A growing reliance on debt to fund AI infrastructure ties the tech trade more closely to the rates outlook, so hawkish central bank signals, including a Fed on a hiking path, could weigh harder on capex-heavy names than in earlier phases of the boom. Credit markets are likely to see heavier tech bond issuance, and investors may demand wider spreads if deployment delays push back revenue. Next week’s Big Tech results are the near-term catalyst: firm capex guidance paired with clearer monetisation would ease funding concerns, while rising spend without visible returns could deepen the mixed share-price reactions already evident. The bank’s preference for diversification points to potential rotation toward sectors and regions outside concentrated US tech leadership.

---

---

The AI build-out is increasingly running on borrowed money, and Standard Chartered wants proof of returns from Big Tech before adding to riskier corners of the sector.

Summary:

  • Standard Chartered says Q3 US tech earnings point to strong compute demand and continued growth in capital spending
  • The bank keeps a positive long-term view on AI investment but flags short-term funding and execution risks, and prefers not to add exposure to higher-risk tech for now
  • It expects debt-financed AI capex to rise from about 25% of the total in 2026 to around 40% in 2027, increasing sensitivity to interest rates
  • Deployment delays could defer revenue while financing costs continue, though wider commercial adoption of AI could generate cash flow and reduce reliance on borrowing
  • Next week’s Big Tech earnings will be assessed for capex guidance, funding and monetisation trends, with market leadership concentrated and share-price reactions mixed
  • The bank remains invested but defensively positioned, favouring diversification across sectors and regions

Third-quarter earnings from US technology companies point to robust demand for computing power and ongoing expansion in capital expenditure, but the growing role of debt in funding the artificial intelligence build-out is adding new risks, according to Standard Chartered.

In its weekly market review, the bank said it retains a favourable long-term view on AI investment, while warning about funding and execution risks in the near term. For now, it prefers not to increase exposure to the higher-risk parts of the technology sector. Recent results suggest that major tech companies remain committed to expanding their AI infrastructure, the bank said.

The central concern is how that expansion is being paid for. Standard Chartered expects borrowing to take on a larger share of the burden as companies spend more on data centres and computing equipment. It forecasts that debt-financed AI capex will rise from about a quarter of total AI capex in 2026 to around 40% in 2027. Greater dependence on debt makes the sector more sensitive to interest rates, the bank said, while any delays in deploying new capacity could push back revenue recognition even as financing costs continue to build.

There is a potential offset. The bank expects broader commercial adoption of AI services to generate additional cash flow, which could help companies fund further infrastructure investment with less need for external borrowing.

That makes next week’s Big Tech earnings a key test. Standard Chartered said it will look to the results for greater clarity on capex guidance, funding plans and progress in monetising AI. It noted that the reporting season carries added uncertainty, with market leadership still concentrated in a small group of stocks and share-price reactions becoming more mixed.

Looking further ahead, the bank expects equity performance to depend more on companies delivering stronger earnings than on further expansion in valuations. It highlighted sustainable AI financing, commercial returns on infrastructure spending and broader profit growth beyond technology as the factors investors should watch. Standard Chartered said it remains invested but defensively positioned, favouring diversification across sectors and regions.

item.title: BOJ preview: Daiwa sees hold, but 2% inflation call could open door to December hike
item.description:
A hold is largely the base case, so the yen and JGB yields are likely to take their cue from the language rather than the decision. A formal declaration that underlying inflation has reached 2%, a Takata dissent and any shift by Ueda toward “next meeting” phrasing would together read as hawkish, supporting the yen and pushing short-end yields higher as markets price a December move. Higher crude prices are a key upside risk, with oil already reigniting upstream cost pressure and feeding the BOJ’s concern about inflation overshooting. A guarded Ueda who stresses a broad review of financial conditions could see December pricing trimmed and the yen soften.

---

Also this week:

  • Preview: RBNZ set to lift OCR to 3% ahead of election as oil and weak kiwi fuel inflation

--- The BOJ is expected to stand pat on rates while quietly moving the goalposts, from getting inflation up to 2% to stopping it from running beyond it, which keeps December firmly in play.

Summary:

  • Daiwa expects the BOJ to keep rates unchanged at its October meeting, with October surveys showing softer household and business inflation expectations
  • The board is likely to conclude that underlying inflation has reached 2%, shifting policy from lifting inflation toward stabilising it around that level
  • Board member Hajime Takata may again propose a rate hike, while Naoki Tamura is seen backing a hold after September’s increase
  • Daiwa expects the Outlook Report to raise the FY26 growth forecast to 0.8% from 0.6% and FY27 core CPI to 2.5% from 2.4%, and to trim FY26 core-core CPI to 2.4%
  • Higher crude prices have reignited upstream inflation pressure, and the BOJ’s policy rate already sits above the lower end of its estimated neutral range of around 1% to 2.5%
  • Ueda’s press conference will be watched for December hints, particularly any shift from “every meeting” language toward the next meeting

The Bank of Japan is expected to leave interest rates unchanged at its October meeting, but the decision could still mark an important shift in its policy thinking, according to a preview from Daiwa Securities. The broker expects the board to conclude that underlying inflation has reached 2%, a step that would move the central bank from a phase of lifting inflation toward its target to one focused on keeping it stable around that level.

Daiwa cited media reports that economic conditions and prices have continued to track the BOJ’s outlook since September, and that policymakers do not see upside inflation risks as strong enough to justify back-to-back rate increases. Surveys published in October also showed inflation expectations among households and businesses easing. Even so, concern about an inflation overshoot remains high. Cost pass-through is broadening at the consumer level, and rising crude oil prices have revived upstream price pressures, with some within the BOJ expecting pass-through to accelerate into next year.

Governor Kazuo Ueda signalled the change in tone earlier this month, saying that with underlying inflation now close to 2%, the bank can no longer tolerate further increases and is aiming to stabilise it. Daiwa expects the Outlook Report to replace its description of inflation as approaching 2% with wording that it is broadly consistent with the target, and argues that if the report continues to flag upside inflation risks, that would provide grounds for considering an early hike.

The broker expects board member Hajime Takata to dissent and propose a hike, as he did in July, citing strong global demand, including for AI-related products. Naoki Tamura, who has spoken of raising rates every few months toward a neutral level of around 2%, is seen supporting a hold so soon after September’s increase.

On forecasts, Daiwa expects the board to lift its FY26 growth projection to 0.8% from 0.6% and FY27 core inflation to 2.5% from 2.4% on the back of higher oil prices, while trimming FY26 core-core inflation slightly to 2.4%. The report is unlikely to factor in a planned cut to the consumption tax on food, which Daiwa estimates could lower core inflation by roughly 1.5 percentage points in FY27.

Ueda’s post-meeting press conference will be pivotal. Daiwa will watch whether he keeps describing rate decisions as being made at each meeting or shifts toward language pointing to the next meeting, which markets could read as a stronger signal of a December hike. With the policy rate already above the lower end of the BOJ’s estimated neutral range, his assessment of financial conditions will also shape expectations for how quickly further tightening follows.

The chart plots the value of the company’s holdings over time, and each orange dot marks a purchase. The graphic has historically come before a Monday 8-K filing confirming that Strategy bought bitcoin the previous week. The caption changes each week, but the message is usually the same: more coins are coming. Over the past two weeks, Saylor captioned the chart with variations on finding room for more orange, and both posts were followed by purchase disclosures. The pattern is not a fixed rule. In July, after a large bitcoin sale, Saylor posted the tracker with an unusually vague caption saying the orange dots tell only part of the story, and the post a week earlier had come before the largest sale in company history. A missing chart suggests a pause, but it does not prove one. The buying has already slowedThe size of recent purchases is the bigger story. Strategy bought 267 BTC for about $22.1 million at an average of $82,900 per coin in the week to October 18. That followed a 250 BTC purchase for about $21.5 million the week before. Earlier in the year, single weekly purchases topped 20,000 BTC. The latest purchase was funded almost entirely by selling 140,872 MSTR shares through the company’s at-the-market program. Over the same week, the company spent far more on its own securities. It used $193.1 million to buy back 1.94 million shares of its STRC preferred stock, and the board raised its digital credit securities repurchase program from $2 billion to $3 billion. STRC is one of Strategy’s preferred shares, which pay holders a regular dividend. Buying them back below their $100 face value reduces the company’s future dividend costs. Michael Saylor 'Found More Room for Orange' as Strategy Adds 267 Bitcoin - Strategy (NASDAQ:MSTR) - BenzingaStrategy has also sold bitcoin this year. It reported selling 32 BTC in early June, its first disclosed sale since a 2022 tax-loss transaction. It then sold 3,588 BTC for about $216 million to fund preferred stock distributions and top up its US dollar reserve. A further 1,638 BTC was sold between July 27 and August 2 at an average of $63,957, with the proceeds split between preferred dividends and STRC buybacks. Even so, Strategy’s holdings stand at 848,517 BTC, bought for about $64 billion at an average of $75,446 per coin, more than 4% of bitcoin’s total supply. What could change the readA pause would not be new. In September, Saylor’s chart returned after a two-week buying break, and purchases resumed. The company also has the money to buy. As of October 4, its USD Reserve stood at $4.88 billion, with $833.4 million in USD Cash. A larger purchase disclosed on Monday would undercut the slowdown story. Another quiet week on bitcoin, alongside continued buybacks, would reinforce it. bitcoinWhat to watch nextThe first test is Monday’s 8-K filing, which will show whether Strategy bought, sold or held bitcoin last week, and how much it spent on buybacks.Next come third-quarter results. Strategy reports after the US close on Thursday, October 29, and will host a live webinar at 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time. The headline profit should hold few surprises, since the fair value of the company’s bitcoin was already above its cost basis as of September 30. Management’s comments on funding, dividends and the balance between buybacks and bitcoin purchases are likely to matter more. For bitcoin traders, the practical point is that Strategy has been a steady buyer through much of this cycle. If its weekly purchases stay small, the market loses a reliable source of demand. Watch the size of the purchases, not just whether there are any.
